extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, philosophers of science, and graduate students interested in explanation and ontology in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess criteria that make a use of mathematics explanatory either in scientific contexts or within mathematics, including issues of indispensability, explanatory power, causal vs non-causal accounts, and the role of abstraction/generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two senses of 'mathematical explanation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical explanation may mean (1) explanations in the natural or social sciences where mathematical facts play an essential role in the explanation, or (2) explanation within mathematics itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this basic distinction to classify cases and to frame subsequent philosophical questions (e.g., applicability and ontology differ across the two senses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner's criterion for mathematical explanation in science
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical explanation of a physical fact is one in which when we remove the physics what we are left with is a mathematical explanation of a mathematical fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner illustrated this with the rigid-body rotation result. Use this as a test for whether the mathematical component is 'essential' to the scientific explanation rather than merely convenient modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential-role requirement (mathematics not dispensable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics counts as explanatory in a scientific explanation when it plays an essential role (i.e., the explanans would not remain explanatory if the mathematical component were removed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast genuinely mathematical explanations with cases where mathematics is merely a convenient description; examine whether removing or replacing the math removes explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical explanations can be non-causal
rubrics_metrics.description: There appear to be physical explanations that are non-causal: geometrical or mathematical facts can explain physical distributions without being causes (Lipton's sticks example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat non-causal explanatory status as a genuine category that may challenge causal theories of explanation; evaluate whether the mathematical facts 'represent' or 'model' the physical situation adequately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability / hooking-on requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounting for mathematical explanations requires an account of how mathematics 'hooks on' to reality—issues of modeling, idealization, and representation are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a purported mathematical explanation, analyze how the mathematical structures map to the physical system and whether that mapping secures the explanatory connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indispensability/ontological commitment strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Indispensability arguments run: mathematics is indispensable to our best science; we should accept scientific theories; therefore accept the entities quantified over by those theories. Baker's version focuses on cases where mathematical postulation increases theoretical virtues, notably explanatory power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples where positing mathematical objects demonstrably improves explanatory virtues (e.g., Baker's cicada case) to assess the force of the indispensability move; consider holistic vs. non-holistic formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power as a theoretical virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: One way mathematical postulates may justify ontological commitment is by increasing explanatory power; explanatoriness is treated as a theoretical virtue that can ground belief in mathematical entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the mathematical component genuinely provides explanatory insight (not just fit or convenience) and whether that increase in explanatory power justifies ontological commitment in the context at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of explanans and realism worry (Leng's objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if there are genuine mathematical explanations of empirical phenomena, this need not commit us to the real existence of mathematical posits because mathematical explanations might not require true explanans or might be satisfiable by fictional/Eliminativist reconstruals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using explanatory role to argue for realism, address whether the explanans must be true and whether mathematical claims involved can be paraphrased or eliminated without loss of explanatory status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for detailed case studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding mathematical explanations (both in science and in mathematics) requires careful, detailed case studies to reveal the varieties of explanatory use and their philosophical consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical/philosophical analysis of exemplars (e.g., Lipton, Steiner, Baker, Batterman) is essential before generalizing about indispensability, applicability, or explanatory categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feferman-style abstraction/generalization justification
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument for belief in certain mathematical entities: (1) scattered results call for explanation; (2) explanation is obtained by appealing to more abstract entities (ideals, analytic functions); (3) this gives reason to postulate those abstract entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this schema to evaluate internal mathematical cases where invoking abstract structures yields unifying/simplifying explanations of disparate data; examine whether such abstraction increases understanding enough to warrant ontological commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivability vs explanatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a result can be derived in a weaker theory (i.e., the abstract entities are in principle eliminable), if the derivation loses explanatory power then the appeal to the abstract entities may be justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a purported explanatory account is reducible, check whether the reduction preserves explanatory virtues; if not, the original (stronger) account may have independent justificatory force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic/structural mathematical explanations (Batterman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mathematical explanations in science are asymptotic: they illuminate structurally stable aspects of a phenomenon and its governing equations via sophisticated mathematical manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize asymptotic explanations as a class (e.g., scaling limits, universality) and evaluate whether they provide genuine explanatory understanding of phenomena beyond mere calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probing the explanatory role: questions to ask
rubrics_metrics.description: When a diagrammatic or mathematical occurrence prompts probing, relevant questions include: (i) is this a breakdown of appearance/control? (ii) which free metric choices lead to the outcome? (iii) what other appearances arise from different choices? (iv) what is the range of control possibilities and outcomes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these probing questions as a methodological rubric when analyzing diagram-based or constructive explanations to ascertain robustness, dependence on idealization, and scope of the explanation.
